article_title: Visual short-term memory through the lifespan: Preserved benefits of context and metacognition.
citation: Daniel J. Mitchell, Cam-CAN (Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience), Rhodri Cusack. (2018). Visual Short-Term Memory Through the Lifespan: Preserved Benefits of Context and Metacognition. Psychology and Aging. https://doi.org/10.1037/pag0000265
title: Mixture-model decomposition of VSTM performance into quantity, quality, and misbinding components
description: The article frames VSTM performance using a continuous color-report paradigm in which a mixture model separates distinct components of performance. As the article states, it fitted a mixture model to the error distribution to give measures of VSTM quantity (K, the expected number of items stored), quality (the precision of items held in memory) and misbinding (the probability of reporting a correct color from a wrong location). The model combines a uniform guessing component with von Mises distributions centered on target and nontarget colors, allowing age-related change to be localized to specific memory components rather than a single aggregate score.
requirements: A continuous report task with response errors measured in color-wheel degrees, fitted with maximum-likelihood mixture model estimation using multiple starting points to avoid local minima.
constraints: K is interpreted empirically as the expected number of items stored without taking a theoretical position on whether storage involves discrete slots or an infinitely divisible resource.
target_learning_goals: measuring the quantity, quality, and binding accuracy of visual short-term memory representations
examples: The model was fit per participant and memory load, separately for trials with and without probe context, and also to a no-memory control block to estimate sensorimotor ability.
key_sources: Daniel J. Mitchell, Cam-CAN (Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience), Rhodri Cusack. (2018). Visual Short-Term Memory Through the Lifespan: Preserved Benefits of Context and Metacognition. Psychology and Aging. https://doi.org/10.1037/pag0000265

article_title: Enhancing students’ dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation
citation: Pengjin Wang · Fan Chen · Deliang Wang · Gaowei Chen (2025). Enhancing students' dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09443-2
title: Four-stage visualisation-supported dialogic reflection (VSDR) implementation cycle
description: VSDR unfolded in four stages across the intervention: teachers record lesson videos; the research team processes videos into visual representations of talk; teachers individually review clips and select segments with relevant visualisations, devising reflection prompts around "'what happened' (facts), 'how to interpret' (reason and evaluation) and 'how to improve' (plan)"; and students use iPads in class to reflect on a discussion forum, reviewing peers' responses and contributing feedback. The pattern mediates students' reflection on classroom talk through context-based group discussion supported by visualised representations.
requirements: Discussion forum with teacher-crafted prompts and technical support for students
Visualised representations integrated with classroom activity videos
constraints: Teachers recorded lessons at different doses (weekly vs bi-weekly), constituting higher- and lower-dose groups rather than a treatment–control contrast
target_learners: primary school students (grade two, around age 7)
target_learning_goals: dialogic reflection on group work and whole-class talk
examples: Hazel's group recorded weekly (14 visualisations) and Leo's bi-weekly (8 visualisations) over three months
key_sources: Pengjin Wang · Fan Chen · Deliang Wang · Gaowei Chen (2025). Enhancing students' dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09443-2

article_title: Nursing students' experiences in virtual simulation teaching: a meta-synthesis of qualitative research.
citation: Zhang Guoyong, Sun Xianghong, Yang Dan, Shao Qinwen. (2026). Nursing students’ experiences in virtual simulation teaching: a meta-synthesis of qualitative research. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1863553
title: Four-theme synthesized framework of nursing students' virtual simulation teaching experiences
description: A qualitative meta-synthesis framework organizing nursing students' experiences of VS teaching into four synthesized findings: "(1) emotional experiences; (2) advantages of VS teaching; (3) challenges of VS teaching; (4) students’ needs for VS teaching." It was built by integrating 65 themes and 156 sub-themes from 17 qualitative studies into nine categories through repeated comparison and thematic analysis following the JBI meta-aggregation approach. The framework serves as a theoretical foundation for optimizing VS teaching equipment and accommodating diverse cultural backgrounds and learning foundations in future educational design.
requirements: Qualitative primary studies of nursing students' experiences in VS teaching environments, appraised with the JBI checklist and rated A or B
constraints: Only Chinese and English databases were searched, and included studies were predominantly from Asian and European countries, limiting adaptability of conclusions to multicultural contexts
examples: The synthesis drew on studies using semi-structured interviews and focus groups across computer-based and immersive VR platforms in eight countries
key_sources: Zhang Guoyong, Sun Xianghong, Yang Dan, Shao Qinwen. (2026). Nursing students’ experiences in virtual simulation teaching: a meta-synthesis of qualitative research. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1863553

article_title: Effectiveness of Virtual Simulations Versus Mannequins and Real Persons in Medical and Nursing Education: Meta-Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
citation: Jiang N, Zhang Y, Liang S, Lyu X, Chen S, Huang X, Pan H. (2024). Effectiveness of Virtual Simulations Versus Mannequins and Real Persons in Medical and Nursing Education: Meta-Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/56195
title: Adopt virtual simulations as viable alternatives to face-to-face simulation where cost-utility and time-space flexibility matter
description: The article concludes that, given "favorable cost-utility plus high flexibility regarding time and space, VSs are viable alternatives to traditional face-to-face learning modalities." This rests on its meta-analytic finding of no significant effectiveness differences across four competencies, plus cited advantages: reduced instructor time, manpower, and space costs, repeatable training without patient harm, and automated documentation and evaluation of student performance.
requirements: Institutions must accept that comparative effectiveness evidence shows equivalence rather than superiority over mannequins and real persons
constraints: The article states the comparative effectiveness of VSs deserves follow-up as new technology emerges, and that undesirable usability may hinder the learning process
target_learners: pre- and postregistration medical and nursing students and staff
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 27 RCTs with 1480 participants comparing VSs to mannequins or real persons, finding no significant differences on any of the four outcomes
key_sources: Jiang N, Zhang Y, Liang S, Lyu X, Chen S, Huang X, Pan H. (2024). Effectiveness of Virtual Simulations Versus Mannequins and Real Persons in Medical and Nursing Education: Meta-Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/56195

article_title: Using the Vocabulary Self-Collection Strategy plus to Develop University EFL Students' Vocabulary Learning
citation: Manal Mohamed Khodary. (2017). Using the Vocabulary Self-Collection Strategy Plus to Develop University EFL Students' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p135
title: VSSPlus: a post-reading vocabulary strategy integrating technological tools with the Vocabulary Self-Collection Strategy
description: VSSPlus is described as a post-reading variant of Haggard's Vocabulary Self-Collection Strategy that adds technological tools. Students select words from a text, answer three questions about each word, and use tools such as e-Dictionaries, Wordsift, Thinglink, podcasts and wikis to explore meanings, synonyms and definitions. The article states it "requires from its users to integrate various applications of technological tools during its practice" and that technology should be applied generatively, with the instructor acting as a facilitator of discussion, word selection and team formation.
requirements: Occurs after reading a selected reading material
Technology applied in a generative way to satisfy learners' learning needs and interests
Instructor facilitates oral discussion, word selection and distributing students into small teams
constraints: The article notes VSSPlus is still a new strategy, with only suggested procedures by Grisham, Wolsey and Smetana (2013) prior to this study
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning and deep comprehension of selected words
examples: The experimental group completed an introductory session plus sessions making an e-Dictionary, a Wordsift and a Thinglink, working in teams of 4 students
key_sources: Manal Mohamed Khodary. (2017). Using the Vocabulary Self-Collection Strategy Plus to Develop University EFL Students' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p135

article_title: Using the Vocabulary Self-Collection Strategy plus to Develop University EFL Students' Vocabulary Learning
citation: Manal Mohamed Khodary. (2017). Using the Vocabulary Self-Collection Strategy Plus to Develop University EFL Students' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p135
title: VSSPlus session sequence: word selection with three questions followed by technology-mediated word-study artifacts
description: The article's training sessions follow a repeated design: teams read a text, select an unknown word, ask and answer three questions (where the word is found, what it means, why it is important to learn it), then produce a technology artifact — an e-Dictionary page with audio recording, a Wordsift visual linking synonyms, or a Thinglink image with tagged definitions and a podcast — and present it to other teams. The article describes sessions in which "each team to co-operate together to select from the previously post-reading text another word" and present it via PPT for discussion.
requirements: Small teams of about 4 students with exchangeable roles
Reading texts containing unknown vocabulary appropriate to learners' level
Access to technological tools (wikis, PPT, audio recording, Wordsift, Thinglink, Podbean)
constraints: Validated in the article for first-level university EFL students in a Vocabulary Building course
target_learning_goals: selecting, defining and using new vocabulary in correct sentences
examples: In the e-Dictionary session, teams used Wikispaces to build dictionary pages with definitions, images and audio recordings of their selected words
key_sources: Manal Mohamed Khodary. (2017). Using the Vocabulary Self-Collection Strategy Plus to Develop University EFL Students' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p135

article_title: Vocabulary Learning through an Online Computerized Flashcard Site
citation: McLean, S., Hogg, N., & Rush, T. W. (2013). Vocabulary learning through an online computerized flashcard site. The JALT CALL Journal, 9(1), 79-98. https://jaltcall.org
title: 80-item Vocabulary Size Test (VST) measuring written receptive vocabulary to the eighth 1000-word level
description: The Vocabulary Size Test (Nation & Beglar, 2007) is a multiple-choice instrument measuring second language English learners' written receptive vocabulary size in word-family units. The study used an 80-item version covering "the first 1000 to the eighth 1000-word families of English", with items based on the 10 million token spoken section of the British National Corpus. Each item presents the target word in a short non-defining context sentence with four substitutable options written in restricted defining vocabulary.
requirements: Administration time limits the version used; the full 14,000-word version requires more class time and may allow more guessing
constraints: The 80-item version tests only up to the 8,000-word level, so gains beyond that level escaped notice, creating a potential ceiling effect that most affected the highest-scoring vocabulary group
target_learners: second language English learners, here first-year Japanese university students
target_learning_goals: estimation of written receptive vocabulary size from the first to eighth 1000-word families
examples: Administered as pretest in the first week of April and posttest in the last week of December, with students incomplete on either test excluded from the dataset
key_sources: McLean, S., Hogg, N., & Rush, T. W. (2013). Vocabulary learning through an online computerized flashcard site. The JALT CALL Journal, 9(1), 79-98. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1108008

article_title: The Use of Video Self-Monitoring Embedded with Mentorship as a Medium to Enhance Experiential Learning Opportunities and Promote Critical Thinking Skills for Educators and Health Science Professionals Working with Children with Autism
citation: Lina Slim-Topdjian & Genevieve Pinto Zipp (2016). The Use of Video Self-Monitoring Embedded with Mentorship as a Medium to Enhance Experiential Learning Opportunities and Promote Critical Thinking Skills for Educators and Health Science Professionals Working with Children with Autism. Global Education Review, 3(4), 6-18. https://ger.mercy.edu
title: Experiential teacher training package combining video self-monitoring, performance feedback, and reflection
description: The article describes an experiential learning teacher/educator training package in which "Video self-monitoring (VSM) is one type of learning strategy used in experiential learning environments to develop critical thinking by building on direct experiences, performance feedback (PF), and reflection (R)". Teachers are videotaped instructing a student, score their own performance against a procedural checklist, receive corrective feedback, and complete a written reflection journal, following Haynes's steps of experiential learning. The package was applied to train teachers of children with autism on learn unit implementation and rate of effective instruction.
requirements: Videotaped teacher-student interactions scored with the TPRA Abbreviated Version against a procedural checklist
A written reflection journal completed after the performance feedback session
constraints: The study did not conduct a component analysis, so the independent effect of reflective processes on teacher behavior was not assessed
target_learners: student teachers and educators of children with autism
target_learning_goals: critical thinking and error detection skills
examples: Teachers were videotaped for three minutes, scored their own performance on the TPRA form with a mentor present, and completed a written reflection journal over four consecutive 15-minute daily sessions
key_sources: Lina Slim-Topdjian & Genevieve Pinto Zipp (2016). The Use of Video Self-Monitoring Embedded with Mentorship as a Medium to Enhance Experiential Learning Opportunities and Promote Critical Thinking Skills for Educators and Health Science Professionals Working with Children with Autism. Global Education Review, 3(4), 6-18. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1120743

article_title: The Effect of Virtual Simulation Game on the Development of Nursing Students' Knowledge and Skills: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Mercan Annak, İ., and Bulut, H. 2026. "The Effect of Virtual Simulation Game on the Development of Nursing Students' Knowledge and Skills: A Randomized Controlled Trial." Nursing Open 13, no. 5: e70566. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70566
title: VSG for Preventing CAUTI: a Unity 3D virtual simulation game in which students play a nurse through four catheter-care stages
description: The researchers developed a screen-based virtual simulation game combining simulation and serious gaming, built "using Unity 3D's real‐time physics engine and the C# software language". The student plays Inci Nurse caring for patient Mr. Salim across four stages, from urine drainage and mobilization to sterile sample collection and catheter removal, with in-game questions and explanatory feedback. Development followed INACSL simulation design standards in five phases: analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation.
requirements: Developed following the INACSL Healthcare Simulation Standards of Best Practice Simulation Design
Educational content validated by nine expert faculty (CVR 0.778–1.00; CVI 0.96–0.99)
constraints: Requires internet access and sufficient device memory; students reported freezing when these were lacking
target_learning_goals: knowledge and skills for preventing catheter-associated urinary tract infection, including catheter care procedures
examples: Students played the game for 7 days on computers or mobile devices, repeating steps as desired; the game blocked progression until the correct operation was performed
key_sources: Mercan Annak, İ., and Bulut, H. 2026. "The Effect of Virtual Simulation Game on the Development of Nursing Students' Knowledge and Skills: A Randomized Controlled Trial." Nursing Open 13, no. 5: e70566. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70566

article_title: Virtual simulation experiments in medical education: technology acceptance, learning outcomes, and motivational impacts.
citation: Li Kaiyue, Li Qun, Wang Linding, Wang Xiaonan, Ding Xiaojuan, Liu Boyu. (2025). Virtual simulation experiments in medical education: technology acceptance, learning outcomes, and motivational impacts. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08025-6
title: Bespoke VSE system for isolation and identification of enteric pathogens structured on Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle
description: A bespoke, in-house virtual simulation platform developed with microbiology faculty that simulates isolation, culture, and identification of enteric pathogens. "Our VSE system is specifically employed to simulate the isolation and identification of enteric pathogens, utilizing virtual reality technology to deliver intuitive and structured operational workflow." Its pedagogy follows Kolb's four phases: concrete experience in simulated labs, reflective observation via system-generated guiding questions and a recording function, abstract conceptualization through experimental report writing, and evaluation and revision with immediate feedback. Students can repeat procedures, adjust viewpoints, and receive step-level feedback.
requirements: Technical support and educator training so the system functions as a supported learning environment
Familiarization training for students before use
constraints: The authors note its structured nature may limit independent judgment because students rely on system feedback rather than their own problem-solving
target_learners: second- and third-year medical and medical laboratory technology students
target_learning_goals: experimental procedure skills in medical microbiology
integration of practical operations with theoretical knowledge
examples: Students practiced sample inoculation, microscopic observation, medium selection, biochemical reactions, and serological tests, and the system automatically generated reflective prompts after each step
key_sources: Li Kaiyue, Li Qun, Wang Linding, Wang Xiaonan, Ding Xiaojuan, Liu Boyu. (2025). Virtual simulation experiments in medical education: technology acceptance, learning outcomes, and motivational impacts. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08025-6

article_title: Application of virtual simulations in the practical teaching of clinical microbiology laboratory courses.
citation: Wang Jiaxue, Jiang Yunshui, Yang Jun, Zhou Qian, Hu Hui, Chen Yan, Jiang Jinqin. (2025). Application of virtual simulations in the practical teaching of clinical microbiology laboratory courses. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07603-y
title: Desktop-based VSO platform for BSL-3 SARS-CoV-2 isolation and culture in clinical microbiology laboratory teaching
description: A browser-based, desktop virtual simulation operation platform developed by the teaching team for SARS-CoV-2 isolation and culture under BSL-3 standards, operated "through conventional keyboard and mouse inputs" without plugins or installation. It contains five learning modules (BSL-3 facility requirements, standard operating procedures, specimen collection and processing, virus isolation and culture, medical waste disposal), gamified task-driven scoring, pop-up quizzes with real-time corrective feedback, and an optional comprehensive assessment module. Three discipline modules cover bacteriology, mycology, and virology.
requirements: Runs in multiple browsers via link-sharing without downloading or additional software; students use registered or guest accounts
constraints: Students reported server instability, interface responsiveness issues, and buffering; the platform provides limited emotional interaction compared with traditional teaching
target_learning_goals: operational skills for pathogen isolation and culture
examples: Used within a BOPPPS-structured blended design: pre-class VSO assignments, in-class offline practical projects, and real-time in-platform assessment
key_sources: Wang Jiaxue, Jiang Yunshui, Yang Jun, Zhou Qian, Hu Hui, Chen Yan, Jiang Jinqin. (2025). Application of virtual simulations in the practical teaching of clinical microbiology laboratory courses. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07603-y

article_title: Development of a GPT-4-Powered Virtual Simulated Patient and Communication Training Platform for Medical Students to Practice Discussing Abnormal Mammogram Results With Patients: Multiphase Study.
citation: Mavragani A, Chan S, Doyle AJ, Weisman D, Sugarman A, Huang YM, Gelberg L, Ganz PA, Comulada WS. (2025). Development of a GPT-4–Powered Virtual Simulated Patient and Communication Training Platform for Medical Students to Practice Discussing Abnormal Mammogram Results With Patients: Multiphase Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/65670
title: Three-component prompt construction framework for LLM-driven virtual simulated patients
description: The article's account of structuring an LLM role-play prompt so the virtual simulated patient behaves like a real patient. "The prompt included (1) context (details about the patient's backstory and medical situation), (2) behavioral instruction (including the patient's emotional state at the time of the phone call with the physician), and (3) constraints (expected patient responses to specific learner choices)." Context was adapted from formative interviews and anonymized chart data; constraints gate scenario objectives, such as refusing to schedule a biopsy without clear explanation.
requirements: Physician review of the prompt to ensure the patient backstory and medical context are representative
Iterative testing across learner types, including deliberately improper communicators, to add constraints addressing undesired behavior
constraints: Prompt improvements identified through heuristic trial and error may have been random conversation variations rather than direct results of prompt changes, as the authors state
target_learning_goals: role-play fidelity to real patient behavior
examples: Prompt text instructed the VSP to become irate if treated without respect, to engage in small talk for rapport building, and to remain in the patient role if prompted to switch.
key_sources: Mavragani A, Chan S, Doyle AJ, Weisman D, Sugarman A, Huang YM, Gelberg L, Ganz PA, Comulada WS. (2025). Development of a GPT-4–Powered Virtual Simulated Patient and Communication Training Platform for Medical Students to Practice Discussing Abnormal Mammogram Results With Patients: Multiphase Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/65670

article_title: Virtual Standardized Patients Versus Traditional Academic Training for Improving Clinical Competence Among Traditional Chinese Medicine Students: Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Yang H, Xiao X, Wu X, Fu X, Du Q, Luo Y, Li B, Zeng J, Zhang Y. (2023). Virtual Standardized Patients Versus Traditional Academic Training for Improving Clinical Competence Among Traditional Chinese Medicine Students: Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/43763
title: VSP-TCM virtual standardized patient system for traditional Chinese medicine clinical training
description: VSP-TCM is a web-based virtual standardized patient application built with Shanghai Dream Road Digital Technology Co. Ltd., using Autodesk Maya for scene and character modeling and Adobe Animate CC for program synthesis. Students interact by text or voice with computerized patients, and the system "simulated a clinical diagnosis, including history taking, physical examination, auxiliary examination, diagnosis and differential diagnosis, and treatment," then summarizes knowledge and evaluates performance in real time. It was developed from a prequestionnaire of students who had taken the PTC-IMTCM course and integrated into that course as the experimental training condition.
requirements: A computer with Microsoft Windows 7 or higher and Microsoft Internet Explorer 8.0 or higher, headsets with microphones, and a case database of foundational diseases matching the physician qualification examination outlines
constraints: VSP-TCM cannot convey some physical signs of real patients; TCM-specific pulse conditions can only be displayed through images, preventing real clinical experience in pulse diagnosis
target_learners: second-year traditional Chinese medicine (5+3 integration) undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: TCM clinical competence including history taking, physical examination, diagnosis, syndrome differentiation, and treatment
examples: In the trial, the VSP-TCM group received 36 class hours of VSP-TCM training in which students selected a disease, completed diagnosis and treatment with a VSP within a specified time, and repeated the exercise according to system feedback
key_sources: Yang H, Xiao X, Wu X, Fu X, Du Q, Luo Y, Li B, Zeng J, Zhang Y. (2023). Virtual Standardized Patients Versus Traditional Academic Training for Improving Clinical Competence Among Traditional Chinese Medicine Students: Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/43763
